en.title: Biotechnology: the whole course
en.short: What biotechnology covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas in teaching order, and how to study well.

sections.heading: What biotechnology is
sections.text: Biotechnology is the use of living cells, parts of cells, or biological molecules to make useful products and solve practical problems. It produces medicines, vaccines, enzymes, food ingredients, fuels, crops and treated water, and it supports diagnosis and environmental clean-up. It is not one subject. It brings together biology, chemistry, physics, mathematics, computing and engineering, within ethics, biosafety and the law. The difference from plain biology is the aim: biotechnology asks how a biological system can be controlled, measured and scaled to do a useful job reliably. A laboratory result that works once is not enough; the process must be safe, repeatable and affordable. These notes teach principles and common methods. They do not replace your institution’s laboratory rules, current regulations or a supervisor’s instructions.

sections.heading: How a biotechnology degree is organised
sections.text: Length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, biotechnology is commonly studied as a four-year BSc in universities, though some programmes and modes differ; polytechnics may offer ND or HND awards in biotechnology or related science laboratory technology where approved. In most of the UK, a BSc usually takes three years and an integrated master’s four. In the US, a bachelor’s usually takes four years. A master’s usually takes one to two years. Early years are often shared with biology, chemistry and mathematics. Later years add molecular methods, bioprocessing, applied areas and a project. Some courses include industrial training or a placement. Accreditation and professional recognition differ by country, so check the current regulator and your department.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text: The introductory stage builds the foundation. It starts with cell biology and organelles, the central dogma of DNA, RNA and protein, and genetics and inheritance. Microbiology, biomolecules and biochemistry come next, supported by chemistry for the life sciences. Biostatistics and experimental design teach how to plan and judge experiments. Laboratory techniques and safety cover practical work, and bioinformatics and computing basics introduce data handling. Recombinant DNA and gene cloning, PCR and nucleic acid analysis, and DNA sequencing and genome analysis are central molecular methods. Protein expression and purification, cell culture and tissue culture, and immunology and antibody technology support products and diagnosis. Microbial genetics and strain improvement, fermentation and bioprocess engineering, downstream processing and product recovery, and industrial biotechnology and bioproducts show how laboratory work becomes manufacturing. Applied core topics include environmental, plant and agricultural, medical and pharmaceutical, and food biotechnology. Bioethics, biosafety and regulation, bioinformatics and omics analysis, and biotechnology enterprise and technology transfer connect science to society and business. At master’s level, advanced molecular genetics and genome editing, systems and synthetic biology, metabolic engineering and strain design, and research methods and the dissertation deepen specialisation.

sections.heading: How to study biotechnology
sections.text: Study biotechnology as a set of connected skills, not a list of facts. For each method, learn three things: the principle, the controls, and the common failure. Ask what the negative control shows and what would happen if a reagent were omitted. Redraw diagrams from memory: the cell, a gene, a cloning vector, a PCR cycle, a fermenter and a purification train. Practise calculations for dilutions, concentrations, cell counts and yields, and write the units on every line. Read a protocol before the laboratory session and record what you actually did, not what you meant to do. Keep a glossary of terms and add one example for each. Use bioinformatics tools after you understand the underlying biology, and check their output against a simple expectation. Ethics and regulation are examinable.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text: Common mistakes include memorising definitions without being able to explain a method or interpret a result. Students confuse a gene with a protein, or a plasmid with a chromosome, and they mix up replication, transcription and translation. In the laboratory, poor labelling, contaminated reagents and missing controls spoil results. In calculations, mixing units such as microlitres and millilitres, or forgetting dilution factors, is frequent. Another mistake is assuming a method that works in one organism will work in another. Students also ignore biosafety rules, waste disposal and approval. In written work, they state a conclusion without showing the evidence. They also treat bioinformatics output as correct because it is computer-generated. Check assumptions, controls and units before you trust a result.

keyPoints: Biotechnology uses living systems or their parts to make products and solve problems.
It combines biology with chemistry, computing, engineering, ethics and regulation.
Degree length and awards differ by country and institution, so check your handbook.
The course moves from cell and molecular foundations to core methods, applications and master’s specialisation.
Learn each method by its principle, controls and common failure, and check units and assumptions.
Laboratory safety, biosafety rules and current regulations are part of the subject, not extras.

en.title: Cell biology and organelles
en.short: Cell types, organelle roles, the cell cycle, microscopy and biotech-relevant cell differences.

sections.heading: Cell types
sections.text:
A prokaryotic cell has no membrane-bound nucleus. Its DNA lies in a nucleoid, usually as one circular chromosome, and it may carry small plasmids. Most bacteria also have 70S ribosomes, a peptidoglycan cell wall and often flagella or pili. A eukaryotic cell has a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and 80S ribosomes. Yeasts, fungi, plants and animals are eukaryotic.

This difference matters in biotechnology. Bacteria grow quickly and are easy to engineer, but they cannot carry out some plant or animal modifications, such as adding complex sugar chains to proteins.

sections.heading: Organelles
sections.text:
Organelles are specialised compartments. The nucleus stores DNA and controls gene expression. Ribosomes make proteins. The rough endoplasmic reticulum folds and modifies proteins, while the smooth endoplasmic reticulum makes lipids. The Golgi apparatus sorts and packages molecules. Mitochondria release energy as ATP by aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis in plants and algae. Lysosomes digest waste, and vacuoles store water and solutes. The plasma membrane is a selective barrier, and the cell wall gives shape and support.

In a lab, a scientist comparing hosts notes that E. coli lacks a nucleus, yeast has a chitin wall, a plant cell has chloroplasts and a large vacuole, and an animal cell has no wall.

sections.heading: Cell cycle and division
sections.text: The cell cycle is the sequence from one division to the next. Interphase has G1 (growth), S (DNA replication) and G2 (preparation). M phase includes mitosis, when one nucleus divides into two genetically identical nuclei, and cytokinesis, when the cytoplasm divides. Meiosis makes gametes with half the chromosome number and creates genetic variation. Prokaryotes divide by binary fission.

sections.heading: Microscopy
sections.text: Microscopes magnify and resolve. Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. If a cell appears 2 mm wide at ×400, its actual width is 2 mm ÷ 400 = 0.005 mm = 5 µm. Resolution is the smallest distance between two points that can be seen as separate; it depends on the lens and wavelength, not only on magnification.

keyPoints: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and organelles; eukaryotes have both.
Ribosomes make proteins, mitochondria make ATP, chloroplasts photosynthesise, and the Golgi sorts and packages.
The cell cycle is G1, S, G2 and M; mitosis gives identical nuclei and meiosis gives variable gametes.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size; resolution depends on the lens and wavelength.
Plant cell walls are mainly cellulose, bacterial walls peptidoglycan, and yeast walls chitin.

en.title: The central dogma: DNA, RNA and protein
en.short: DNA structure and replication, transcription, translation, the genetic code and gene control.

sections.heading: DNA and replication
sections.text: DNA is a double helix. Two strands are held by base pairs: A with T, and G with C. Each strand is a chain of nucleotides, each with deoxyribose, phosphate and a base. The strands run in opposite directions, so each can act as a template. Replication is semiconservative: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a new strand only in the 5′ to 3′ direction, giving two molecules, each with one old and one new strand. Repair limits errors; remaining changes are mutations.

sections.heading: Transcription
sections.text: Transcription copies a gene into RNA. RNA polymerase binds a promoter, the start signal, and builds an RNA strand complementary to one DNA strand, using uracil in place of thymine. In eukaryotes the RNA is processed: a cap and poly(A) tail are added and introns are spliced out. The mature mRNA carries the message. tRNA and rRNA help translation; small RNAs can regulate it.

sections.heading: Translation and the code
sections.text: Translation builds protein from mRNA. Each codon, a triplet of bases, specifies an amino acid or a stop signal. The code is read 5′ to 3′ and is degenerate: most amino acids have several codons. tRNA carries an amino acid and pairs its anticodon with the codon. The ribosome links the amino acids. Example: DNA template 3′-TAC-5′ gives mRNA 5′-AUG-3′, the start codon for methionine; AUG changed to UAG gives a stop codon.

sections.heading: Control and targets
sections.text: Expression is controlled mainly at transcription. Transcription factors bind near promoters and raise or lower RNA polymerase activity; bacterial operons switch groups of genes together. After transcription, splicing, mRNA stability, translation efficiency and small RNAs add control. These steps are targets because tools can change when, where or how much a gene is expressed. A strong promoter can increase transcription of a useful gene; RNA interference can block an mRNA. Knowing the central dogma shows where to intervene.

keyPoints: DNA is a double helix with A paired to T and G paired to C; replication is semiconservative.
DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to a new strand in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
Transcription uses RNA polymerase and a promoter to make RNA complementary to one DNA strand.
Translation reads mRNA codons 5′ to 3′; each codon specifies an amino acid or a stop signal.
The genetic code is degenerate; AUG is the start codon for methionine and UAG is a stop codon.
Gene expression is controlled at transcription and after transcription, and many biotechnological tools target these steps.

en.title: Genetics and inheritance
en.short: Mendelian inheritance, linkage and recombination, mutation and DNA repair, and population genetics.

sections.heading: Mendelian inheritance
sections.text: A gene is a DNA segment that controls a trait; its versions are alleles. Diploid organisms carry two alleles per gene, one from each parent. Mendel’s law of segregation says the two alleles separate in meiosis, so each gamete carries one. Independent assortment says alleles of genes on different chromosomes pass independently. A dominant allele shows in a heterozygote; a recessive allele shows only in a homozygote. A monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes gives a 3:1 ratio; two unlinked genes give 9:3:3:1.

sections.heading: Linkage and recombination
sections.text: Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and tend to pass together, breaking independent assortment. Crossing over between homologous chromosomes in meiosis can separate linked alleles. The proportion of recombinant offspring is the recombination frequency. It rises with distance between genes, up to about 50%, where linkage is not detected. A frequency of 1% is one centimorgan (cM). Linkage maps use these frequencies. Breeders use recombination to combine desirable alleles, but linked undesirable alleles may come too.

sections.heading: Mutation and DNA repair
sections.text: A mutation is a change in DNA sequence. Substitutions replace a base; insertions or deletions add or remove bases and can shift the reading frame. A mutation may be silent, missense (one amino acid changed) or nonsense (a stop codon created). Mutations arise spontaneously or from mutagens. Cells repair DNA by mismatch, base excision and nucleotide excision repair, and by homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining for double-strand breaks. Unrepaired mutations create new alleles, supplying variation for selection.

sections.heading: Population genetics
sections.text: Population genetics studies allele frequencies. For two alleles, let p and q be their frequencies, so p + q = 1. Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q². This assumes random mating, a large population, and no selection, mutation or migration. Real populations depart; selection changes allele frequencies. Example: if q = 0.2, then p = 0.8. Heterozygote frequency is 2pq = 2 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.32. Homozygotes are p² = 0.64 and q² = 0.04.

keyPoints: Mendel’s law of segregation separates the two alleles of a gene during meiosis; independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes.
A monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes gives 3:1 with complete dominance; two unlinked genes give 9:3:3:1.
Linked genes lie on the same chromosome; recombination frequency rises with distance and 1% equals 1 cM.
Mutations are DNA sequence changes; repair systems include mismatch, base excision, nucleotide excision and double-strand break repair.
Hardy-Weinberg: p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1 under random mating, large population, no selection, mutation or migration.
If q = 0.2, then p = 0.8 and 2pq = 0.32, so 32% of the population are heterozygotes.

en.title: Microbiology fundamentals: microbes, growth and safe handling
en.short: Microbial groups, growth measurement, culture, staining, sterilisation and safe handling.

sections.heading: Microbial groups
sections.text: Most microbes are living things too small to see clearly without a microscope. Bacteria are prokaryotes: single cells with no nucleus, a cell wall, and circular DNA. Most have one of two wall types, distinguished by Gram staining. Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus; yeasts are single cells, moulds form filaments called hyphae. Viruses are not cells: a protein coat around DNA or RNA, and they reproduce only inside a host cell. Other microbes include protozoa, algae and archaea. Classification uses cell type, cell wall, nutrition and genetic sequence.

sections.heading: Growth and measurement
sections.text: Microbial growth means an increase in cell number, not cell size. In batch culture, a population passes through lag, log, stationary and death phases. Generation time is the time for the population to double. If a culture goes from 1.0 × 10⁵ to 8.0 × 10⁵ cells in 6 hours, it has doubled three times (2³ = 8), so the generation time is 6 ÷ 3 = 2 hours. Measurement methods include viable plate counts, turbidity (optical density), direct microscopy and dry mass. Viable counts measure only living cells; turbidity is quick but needs calibration.

sections.heading: Culture and staining
sections.text: Culture media supply nutrients. Selective media allow some microbes to grow and inhibit others; differential media show a visible difference, such as colour. Isolation spreads a sample so single cells form separate colonies. A colony is a visible mass of cells grown from one cell. Staining increases contrast. Simple stains show shape; differential stains such as Gram stain separate bacteria by cell wall structure. Aseptic technique keeps cultures pure and prevents contamination.

sections.heading: Sterilisation and safety
sections.text: Sterilisation kills or removes all microbes, including spores. Heat, filtration and radiation are common. Disinfection reduces harmful microbes on surfaces but may not kill spores. Antisepsis is disinfection of skin or tissue. Safe handling uses aseptic technique, gloves, containment and correct waste disposal. Work is classified by biosafety level, from low-risk to dangerous pathogens; the exact rules depend on the country and institution, so check the current official guidance.

keyPoints: Bacteria are prokaryotes; fungi are eukaryotes; viruses are not cells and need a host.
Generation time = time ÷ number of doublings, and growth means an increase in cell number.
Viable plate counts measure living cells; turbidity is indirect and needs calibration.
Selective media inhibit some microbes; differential media show a visible difference.
Sterilisation kills all microbes including spores; disinfection reduces harmful microbes and may not kill spores.
Safe handling uses aseptic technique, containment and local biosafety rules.

en.title: Biomolecules and biochemistry
en.short: Proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids, enzyme kinetics and metabolic energy flow.

sections.heading: Molecules in water
sections.text: Water is polar, so it surrounds ions and polar groups (hydrophilic) and pushes nonpolar groups together (hydrophobic). Carbohydrates are sugars or polymers of sugars; they store energy and form structural fibres. Lipids are mostly nonpolar; fats store energy, phospholipids form membranes because they are amphipathic, with a polar head and nonpolar tails. Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides; their bases stack and pair by hydrogen bonds, which lets them store and copy information. Shape follows from weak interactions and determines function.

sections.heading: Proteins and shape
sections.text: Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. The chain folds into a three-dimensional shape held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic packing and disulfide bridges. The shape creates an active site or binding surface. Heat or extreme pH can denature a protein: the weak bonds break and function is lost. A small change in sequence can change shape and function.

sections.heading: Enzymes and kinetics
sections.text: Enzymes are protein catalysts: they speed reactions without being used up and lower activation energy, the energy barrier. The Michaelis-Menten model gives v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]). Vmax is the maximum rate; Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax and measures affinity (lower Km means tighter binding). Competitive inhibitors compete for the active site and raise Km; noncompetitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and lower Vmax. Example: Vmax = 100 µmol/min, Km = 2 mM, [S] = 3 mM. v = 100 × 3 ÷ (2 + 3) = 60 µmol/min.

sections.heading: Energy pathways
sections.text: Metabolism is the linked set of reactions that release or use energy. Glycolysis splits glucose in the cytoplasm and yields ATP and pyruvate. In mitochondria, the Krebs cycle oxidises pyruvate and products of fat breakdown, making NADH and FADH2 and a little ATP; oxidative phosphorylation then uses these carriers to make most of the ATP. ATP is the common energy currency: hydrolysis releases energy for work. Carbohydrates and lipids are main fuels; proteins are used when needed. Energy flows from food to ATP to cellular work.

keyPoints: Hydrophilic groups dissolve in water; hydrophobic groups cluster together, and amphipathic lipids form membranes.
Protein shape is held by weak bonds and disulfide bridges, and shape determines function; denaturation destroys function.
Michaelis-Menten: v = Vmax[S] ÷ (Km + [S]); Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax.
Competitive inhibitors raise Km; noncompetitive inhibitors lower Vmax.
Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation convert food energy into ATP.
ATP is the cell’s common energy currency, linking energy-releasing reactions to work.

en.title: Chemistry for the life sciences
en.short: Functional groups, acids and buffers, dilution, titration and spectrophotometry for laboratory work.

sections.heading: Functional groups
sections.text: Organic functional groups are atom groups that give molecules their reactions. Common groups in living systems are hydroxyl (−OH), carbonyl (C=O, as aldehyde or ketone), carboxyl (−COOH), amino (−NH2), phosphate and sulfhydryl (−SH). Each group has characteristic polarity and reactivity. Reaction types include condensation, where two molecules join and water is lost; hydrolysis, the reverse; oxidation and reduction; acid-base proton transfer; and addition or substitution at carbon. These ideas explain how sugars, fats, proteins and nucleic acids are built and broken down.

sections.heading: Acids and pH
sections.text: An acid donates a proton (H+) and a base accepts one. pH = −log10[H+] for dilute aqueous solutions, with [H+] in mol/L; pH falls as acidity rises. A buffer is a weak acid with its conjugate base, or a weak base with its conjugate acid. It resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added, best near its pKa. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is pH = pKa + log10([A−] ÷ [HA]).

sections.heading: Solutions and dilution
sections.text: Concentration is amount of solute per volume of solution. Molarity, M, is moles per litre. To dilute, use C1V1 = C2V2, where C is concentration and V is volume. Example: to make 100.0 mL of 0.0500 M NaCl from 0.500 M stock, V1 = (0.0500 × 100.0) ÷ 0.500 = 10.0 mL. Add 10.0 mL stock to about 80 mL water, mix, then make up to 100.0 mL. Always use the same units on both sides.

sections.heading: Titration and spectrophotometry
sections.text: Titration delivers a standard solution of known concentration until the reaction is complete. At the equivalence point, the balanced equation relates moles of standard to moles of analyte, the substance being measured. Spectrophotometry measures absorbance A, which follows the Beer-Lambert law A = εcl, where ε is molar absorptivity and l is path length. A blank, the solvent with no analyte, and a calibration curve are used. Example: if A = 0.30, l = 1.00 cm and ε = 1500 L mol−1 cm−1, then c = A ÷ (εl) = 0.30 ÷ 1500 = 2.0 × 10−4 mol/L.

keyPoints: pH = −log10[H+] for dilute aqueous solutions; buffers work best near their pKa.
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log10([A−] ÷ [HA]).
Dilution: C1V1 = C2V2, with consistent units.
Titration uses a standard solution and the balanced equation to find moles of analyte.
Beer-Lambert law: A = εcl; use a blank and a calibration curve.
Functional groups such as carboxyl, amino and hydroxyl determine polarity and reactivity.

en.title: Biostatistics and experimental design
en.short: Descriptive stats, probability, sampling, confidence intervals, t, chi-square, ANOVA, correlation, regression, design.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text:
Descriptive statistics summarise a sample: mean (average), median (middle value) and standard deviation (SD, spread around the mean). Variance is SD squared.

Probability distributions model variation: binomial for success counts in fixed trials, Poisson for rare counts, normal for continuous measurements clustered around a mean. Many tests assume approximate normality or large samples.

sections.heading: Sampling and intervals
sections.text:
Random sampling gives every unit a known chance of selection; stratified sampling draws random samples within groups.

The standard error of a mean is SE = s ÷ √n. A 95% confidence interval is x̄ ± t × SE, with t for n − 1 degrees of freedom. Example: n = 25, x̄ = 10.0, s = 2.0, so SE = 0.4. With t = 2.064, the interval is 10.0 ± 0.826, or 9.17 to 10.83.

sections.heading: Hypothesis tests
sections.text:
A hypothesis test compares null H0 with an alternative. The p-value is the chance of data at least as extreme if H0 is true; reject H0 if p is below the significance level, often 0.05.

The one-sample t-test uses t = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (s ÷ √n); two-sample and paired t-tests compare means. Chi-square compares observed counts O with expected counts E: χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E. ANOVA compares three or more means using the F ratio of between-group to within-group variance. Use t or ANOVA for continuous normal means, chi-square for categorical counts.

sections.heading: Design and regression
sections.text:
Controlled experiments need a control, random allocation, replication and, where possible, blocking (grouping similar units, such as by batch or location, and randomising within each group). Replicates estimate variability and improve precision.

Correlation r measures the strength and direction of a straight-line association between two continuous variables, from −1 to +1. Regression fits y = a + bx to predict y from x; b is the slope. Correlation does not prove causation. Match the test to the design and data, and check independence, normality and equal variance.

keyPoints: Descriptive statistics use mean, median and SD; SD is the square root of variance.
Common probability models are binomial for success counts, Poisson for rare counts and normal for continuous measurements.
Standard error SE = s ÷ √n and a 95% confidence interval is x̄ ± t × SE with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
One-sample t-test: t = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (s ÷ √n); chi-square: χ² = Σ (O − E)² ÷ E; ANOVA uses the F ratio of between-group to within-group variance.
Correlation r runs from −1 to +1; regression fits y = a + bx, but correlation does not prove causation.
Good experiments use a control, random allocation, replication and blocking (grouping similar units); choose the test to match the data type and check assumptions.

en.title: Laboratory techniques and safety
en.short: Aseptic work, measuring, solutions, autoclave, centrifuge, spectrophotometer, safety and records.

sections.heading: Aseptic work and measurement
sections.text:
Aseptic technique keeps unwanted microorganisms out of sterile materials. Work in a clean area or laminar flow hood, sterilise loops and bottle necks, and keep lids on. Never mouth pipette: use a pipette aid, hold the pipette vertically and read the meniscus at eye level. Weigh on a level, tared balance and record the exact mass.

Example: 500 mL of 0.50 M sodium chloride (molar mass 58.44 g/mol).
Moles = 0.50 × 0.500 = 0.250 mol
Mass = 0.250 × 58.44 = 14.61 g
Dissolve and make to 500 mL in a volumetric flask.

sections.heading: Media and instruments
sections.text:
Media are nutrient preparations for cells. Calculate each ingredient, dissolve it, adjust pH if the protocol says so, and sterilise. An autoclave uses steam under pressure, commonly 121 °C; time depends on the load and manufacturer’s instructions. Do not seal bottles; loosen caps. Wait until pressure falls before opening.

A centrifuge separates by density. Balance tubes opposite each other, use tubes rated for the speed, close the lid and wait until it stops. Report speed as relative centrifugal force (RCF), not only rpm.

A spectrophotometer measures absorbance. Set the wavelength, zero with a blank, use a clean cuvette and keep readings in the linear range. Beer-Lambert law: A = εcl.

sections.heading: Safety, records and waste
sections.text:
Before practical work, carry out a risk assessment: identify hazards, decide who may be harmed, and set controls. Hazards include biological agents, chemicals, sharps, fire and electricity. Use personal protective equipment (PPE) such as a lab coat, gloves and eye protection. Wash hands. Know where the fire extinguisher, first-aid kit and spill kit are. Report accidents.

Waste must be segregated. Sharps go in a sharps container; biological waste is autoclaved or disinfected; chemical waste is collected separately. Rules differ by country and institution, so check the current local policy.

Keep a bound notebook in permanent ink. Record date, title, materials, method, observations, raw data, calculations and deviations. Cross out errors with one line and initial them.

keyPoints: Aseptic technique keeps unwanted microorganisms out of sterile materials and cultures.
Never mouth pipette; use a pipette aid and read the meniscus at eye level.
Mass = molarity × volume in litres × molar mass.
Autoclave steam under pressure; do not seal bottles and wait for pressure to fall.
Balance centrifuge tubes, report speed as RCF, and use A = εcl for spectrophotometer readings after zeroing with a blank.
Risk assessment, PPE, waste segregation and a bound notebook are required.

en.title: Bioinformatics and computing basics
en.short: Biological databases, sequence formats, alignment, BLAST, trees and command-line skills.

sections.heading: Databases and formats
sections.text:
Biological databases store sequences and notes. For nucleotides, the public archives are GenBank (NCBI, USA), the European Nucleotide Archive (EMBL-EBI, Europe) and DDBJ (Japan); they exchange data. UniProt holds protein sequences and annotation; the Protein Data Bank (PDB) holds three-dimensional structures.

A sequence file format is a fixed layout for sequence and metadata. FASTA has a header line beginning > then the sequence. FASTQ adds per-base quality scores. GenBank flat files add features and references. Record the accession number, a stable identifier, and the release date, because entries change.

sections.heading: Sequence alignment
sections.text:
Pairwise alignment compares two sequences. A global alignment (Needleman-Wunsch) spans both sequences end to end; a local alignment (Smith-Waterman) finds the best matching region. Both use a scoring scheme: a reward for matching symbols, a penalty for mismatches, and a gap penalty. The score is not a probability.

Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) aligns three or more sequences. Tools include Clustal Omega, MUSCLE and MAFFT. An MSA shows conserved positions, which may suggest function or evolutionary constraint.

sections.heading: BLAST and trees
sections.text:
BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) compares a query with a database. It is heuristic: it finds short exact seeds and extends them, so it is fast but not guaranteed to find the best alignment. BLASTN compares nucleotides, BLASTP proteins, and BLASTX translates a nucleotide query. The E-value is the expected number of chance hits; smaller is more significant.

A phylogenetic tree shows inferred evolutionary relationships. Leaves are sequences or species, branches represent lineages, and a clade is a group descended from one ancestor. Common methods include neighbour joining, which is distance-based, and the character-based maximum parsimony and maximum likelihood. Bootstrap values show support for a branch.

sections.heading: Command line and scripts
sections.text: The command line is a text interface for running programs and joining them with pipes. For example, grep -c "^>" sequences.fasta counts FASTA records, because each record starts with >. Scripts in Python, often with Biopython, automate reading files, running BLAST and parsing results. Keep raw data unchanged and write outputs to new files.

keyPoints: GenBank, ENA and DDBJ are the main nucleotide archives; UniProt holds protein sequences and PDB holds structures.
FASTA stores a header and sequence; FASTQ adds quality scores.
Pairwise alignment uses match rewards, mismatch penalties and gap penalties; global spans whole sequences, local finds the best region.
BLAST is a fast heuristic search; the E-value is the expected number of chance hits, so smaller is more significant.
A phylogenetic tree shows inferred relationships; bootstrap values indicate branch support.
Command-line tools and Python scripts automate sequence file handling and searches.

en.title: Recombinant DNA and gene cloning
en.short: Restriction enzymes, ligases, vectors, transformation, selection, and genomic and cDNA libraries.

sections.heading: Cutting and joining
sections.text:
Restriction endonucleases cut DNA at specific recognition sequences, often palindromic. Type II enzymes are the main cloning tools: they cut the sugar-phosphate backbone and usually leave short single-stranded overhangs called sticky ends, though some leave blunt ends. Complementary sticky ends anneal by base pairing.

DNA ligase then seals the join between a 3'-OH and a 5'-phosphate; T4 DNA ligase is widely used. Alkaline phosphatase removes 5' phosphates so a cut vector cannot re-ligate to itself.

sections.heading: Vectors
sections.text:
A vector carries the insert into a host cell and lets it replicate. A plasmid vector is a small circular DNA with an origin of replication, a selectable marker such as an antibiotic-resistance gene, and a cloning site.

Phage vectors, such as lambda derivatives, accept larger inserts and enter cells efficiently. Cosmids and artificial chromosomes take larger fragments still. The choice depends on insert size and host.

sections.heading: Transformation and selection
sections.text:
Transformation is the uptake of DNA by a host, usually Escherichia coli made competent by calcium ions or electroporation. Selection finds cells that took up a vector: only cells carrying the resistance marker grow on antibiotic medium.

Screening then separates recombinants from empty vectors. In blue-white screening the vector carries lacZ; an insert disrupts it, so recombinant colonies stay white while non-recombinant colonies turn blue on X-gal.

sections.heading: Libraries and workflow
sections.text:
A genomic library is a set of clones covering the whole genome: genomic DNA is cut and all fragments are ligated into vectors. A cDNA library is made by copying mRNA with reverse transcriptase; it holds only expressed genes and no introns.

Workflow: isolate DNA, cut vector and insert, ligate, transform, select, then confirm the clone by restriction mapping, PCR or sequencing.

keyPoints: Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sites, usually leaving sticky ends.
DNA ligase seals the join between a 3'-OH and a 5'-phosphate.
A vector needs an origin of replication, a selectable marker and a cloning site.
Transformation introduces DNA into a host; selection uses the marker to find it.
Blue-white screening uses lacZ disruption to identify recombinants.
Genomic libraries contain all DNA; cDNA libraries contain only expressed genes.

en.title: PCR and nucleic acid analysis
en.short: PCR principles, primer design, real-time and RT-PCR, gels, blots, hybridisation, microarrays and failures.

sections.heading: PCR principles
sections.text: PCR copies a chosen DNA region in repeated cycles. Each cycle has three steps: denaturation, usually 94 to 98 °C, separates the double helix; annealing, usually 50 to 65 °C, lets short single-stranded primers bind the template; extension, usually 72 °C, lets a thermostable DNA polymerase such as Taq add nucleotides from the primers. Repeating about 25 to 35 cycles doubles the product each cycle, so the target grows exponentially. Applications include cloning, diagnosis, forensics and detecting pathogens.

sections.heading: Primers and variants
sections.text: Primers are 18 to 25 nucleotides, with 40 to 60 percent GC, similar melting temperatures and no strong self-complementarity or primer dimers. The 3' end must match the template. Real-time PCR measures fluorescence each cycle; the cycle at which signal crosses a threshold, Ct or Cq, falls as starting template rises, allowing quantification. Reverse-transcription PCR (RT-PCR) first makes cDNA from RNA with reverse transcriptase, then amplifies it; it is used for RNA viruses and gene expression. Applications include viral load, expression studies and mutation detection.

sections.heading: Gels and blots
sections.text: Agarose gel electrophoresis separates DNA or RNA by size. Nucleic acids are negatively charged and move toward the anode through a gel; smaller fragments move faster. A stain and ultraviolet light make bands visible, and a ladder gives sizes. Southern blotting transfers DNA from a gel to a membrane and detects a specific sequence with a labelled probe; Northern blotting does the same for RNA. Applications include checking PCR products, restriction digests, gene copy number and transcript size.

sections.heading: Hybridisation and failures
sections.text: Hybridisation is base pairing between a probe and a complementary target. Microarrays place many probes on a chip and measure which targets bind, usually to compare gene expression between samples. Common PCR failures include inhibitors in the sample, degraded template, wrong annealing temperature, poor primers, missing magnesium or inactive enzyme, and contamination. Blot and microarray failures often come from weak probe labelling, poor transfer, non-specific hybridisation or insufficient washing. Always include controls and check each step.

keyPoints: PCR cycles are denaturation, annealing and extension.
Real-time PCR uses the Ct or Cq value to estimate starting template amount.
RT-PCR converts RNA to cDNA before amplification.
Agarose gel electrophoresis separates nucleic acids mainly by size.
Southern blotting detects DNA and Northern blotting detects RNA after transfer and hybridisation.
Failed PCRs often reflect inhibitors, poor primers, wrong annealing temperature or contamination.

en.title: DNA sequencing and genome analysis
en.short: Sanger and next-generation sequencing, library preparation, assembly, annotation and data checks.

sections.heading: Sanger sequencing
sections.text: Sanger sequencing uses DNA polymerase to copy a template in the presence of a small amount of a dideoxynucleotide, which stops the chain when incorporated. The products are separated by capillary electrophoresis and read as a chromatogram. Each reaction gives one read, so Sanger is used for single genes, PCR products and validation, rarely for whole genomes now.

sections.heading: Next-generation platforms
sections.text: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) reads millions of DNA molecules in parallel. Short-read platforms, such as Illumina sequencing by synthesis, give many accurate reads. Long-read platforms, such as Oxford Nanopore and PacBio, read single molecules and help span repeats. Library preparation turns DNA into a sequencing library: fragment it, add adapters, size-select, amplify and check quality. For RNA-seq, RNA is first converted to cDNA.

sections.heading: Assembly and annotation
sections.text: De novo assembly joins overlapping reads into contigs, then scaffolds. Reference mapping aligns reads to a known genome and calls a consensus. Annotation marks genes and features. It uses open reading frames, homology to known genes, and RNA evidence such as RNA-seq splice junctions. Assembly and annotation are hypotheses until checked.

sections.heading: Coverage and checks
sections.text: Coverage is the average number of times a base is read: coverage = (reads × read length) ÷ genome size. Example: 2,000,000 reads of 150 bp give 300,000,000 bp; over a 30 Mb genome that is 10× coverage. Check Phred quality scores, trim low-quality bases, remove adapters and contamination, and inspect coverage and assembly completeness. Confirm important variants by PCR and Sanger sequencing. RNA-seq data are checked for read quality, then mapped to count transcripts and splice junctions. Interpretation depends on the question: variants need coverage and validation; expression needs replicates and normalisation.

keyPoints: Sanger sequencing reads one DNA fragment at a time by chain termination and capillary electrophoresis.
NGS reads many molecules in parallel; short reads are accurate and long reads span repeats.
Library preparation fragments DNA, adds adapters, selects size, amplifies and checks quality.
De novo assembly builds contigs; reference mapping aligns reads to a known genome.
Coverage = (number of reads × read length) ÷ genome size.
Annotation and variant calls must be checked against quality scores, coverage and independent validation.

en.title: Protein expression and purification
en.short: Making proteins in bacterial, yeast and mammalian hosts, then purifying and checking them.

sections.heading: Expression hosts
sections.text: Heterologous expression means making a protein in a host that does not normally produce it. Escherichia coli is fast and cheap and gives high yields, but it cannot add human-type sugar chains (glycosylation), may fold eukaryotic proteins wrongly, and can form inclusion bodies. Yeast folds many proteins better and can secrete them, though its glycosylation differs from human. Mammalian cells give folding and glycosylation closest to human proteins, but are slow and costly. The choice balances yield, cost, folding and required modifications.

sections.heading: Tags and folding
sections.text: Tags are short peptides or proteins fused to the target to aid detection or purification. A polyhistidine tag (His6) binds nickel or cobalt ions; GST (glutathione S-transferase) and MBP (maltose-binding protein) act as solubility partners; FLAG and GFP (green fluorescent protein) help detection. A protease site allows tag removal. Tags can alter folding or activity. Solubility depends on the protein and conditions. Lowering induction temperature, reducing inducer, co-expressing chaperones, or changing host can help. Misfolded protein may form inclusion bodies, which must be dissolved and refolded, often with low yield.

sections.heading: Purification
sections.text: Purification separates the target from host proteins, nucleic acids and media components. Chromatographic methods include affinity chromatography (capture by a tag or ligand), ion exchange (charge), size exclusion (size) and hydrophobic interaction (surface hydrophobicity). Non-chromatographic methods include salt precipitation, ultrafiltration and aqueous two-phase extraction. A typical process captures, then polishes. For example, a His-tagged enzyme made in E. coli can be captured on nickel resin, washed, eluted with imidazole, then buffer-exchanged. Conditions vary for each protein.

sections.heading: Checking the product
sections.text: SDS-PAGE (sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis) denatures proteins and separates them by mass. It shows size and purity. Western blotting transfers proteins to a membrane and detects a specific protein with an antibody, confirming identity and tag presence. A small case: a lab in Ibadan expresses a His-tagged enzyme in E. coli, finds much in the insoluble pellet, purifies the soluble fraction on nickel resin, and uses SDS-PAGE and an anti-His Western blot to confirm the expected band.

keyPoints: Heterologous expression uses a host that does not normally make the protein; E. coli is fast and cheap but cannot add human-type sugar chains.
Yeast and mammalian cells give better eukaryotic folding, but mammalian cells are slower and more expensive.
Affinity tags such as His6, GST and MBP aid purification or solubility, but can change the protein and may need removal.
Solubility is improved by lowering temperature or inducer, using chaperones, or changing host; misfolded protein may form inclusion bodies.
Purification uses affinity, ion exchange, size exclusion or hydrophobic interaction chromatography, or non-chromatographic steps such as precipitation and ultrafiltration.
SDS-PAGE checks size and purity; Western blotting confirms identity with an antibody.

en.title: Cell culture and tissue culture
en.short: Aseptic animal and plant cell culture, media, cell lines, subculture, cryopreservation and contamination.

sections.heading: Aseptic culture
sections.text:
Aseptic technique means handling cells and media so that only the intended organism grows. Work in a laminar flow cabinet with filtered air, sterilise tools and media, and use sterile gloves.

Animal cells are usually grown in plastic flasks in a humid 37 °C incubator with 5% CO2; plant cultures grow on agar or in liquid medium at about 25 °C under light. Antibiotics are not a substitute for good technique.

sections.heading: Media and conditions
sections.text:
Animal media supply salts, amino acids, vitamins, glucose and a pH buffer, often with serum for growth factors. Plant media, commonly Murashige and Skoog (MS), supply mineral salts, sucrose and hormones; auxin and cytokinin ratios steer root or shoot formation.

Cells need the right pH, temperature, oxygen and density. A case: a student in Ibadan finds her flask cloudy and yellow within a day. That suggests bacterial contamination or a pH fall, not normal growth.

sections.heading: Primary cultures and lines
sections.text:
A primary culture is started directly from tissue and often has a finite lifespan. A cell line is derived from it; a continuous line can divide indefinitely.

Subculture, or passaging, moves cells to fresh medium when they become crowded, using trypsin to detach adherent animal cells. Plant cultures are divided similarly. Cryopreservation stores cells at very low temperature, usually in liquid nitrogen, with a cryoprotectant such as dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) or glycerol and controlled cooling.

sections.heading: Contamination and uses
sections.text:
Contamination may show as turbidity, unusual colour, particles or changed cell shape. Mycoplasma, a tiny bacterium, is invisible under the microscope and needs testing.

Characterise cells by morphology, growth rate, karyotype, surface markers and, for human lines, short tandem repeat (STR) profiling. Cultured cells make vaccines and proteins, test drugs for toxicity, study disease, propagate plants and produce plant metabolites. Check identity and sterility before trusting results.

keyPoints: Aseptic technique and sterile media are essential; antibiotics do not replace them.
Animal cells need buffered media, serum or defined supplements, 37 °C and CO2; plant cultures use MS salts, sucrose, hormones and light.
A primary culture comes from tissue and is finite; a continuous cell line can be subcultured indefinitely.
Subculture uses fresh medium and, for adherent animal cells, trypsin; cryopreservation uses a cryoprotectant and liquid nitrogen.
Contamination can be visible or invisible, so test for mycoplasma and check sterility.
Characterise cells by morphology, growth, karyotype, markers and STR profiling, and use them for vaccines, proteins, drug testing and plant propagation.

en.title: Immunology and antibody technology
en.short: Innate and adaptive immunity, antibody structure, hybridomas, ELISA and immunofluorescence.

sections.heading: Innate and adaptive immunity
sections.text:
Innate immunity is the fast, non-specific first line: barriers, phagocytes, complement proteins and inflammation. It does not improve with repeated exposure.

Adaptive immunity is slower and specific. It recognises particular molecules, called antigens, and keeps memory cells, so a second exposure gives a faster, stronger response. Its two arms are antibody (humoral) and cell-mediated.

sections.heading: Antigens, antibodies, B and T cells
sections.text:
An antigen is any molecule an antibody or T-cell receptor can bind. An antibody (immunoglobulin) is a Y-shaped protein of two heavy and two light chains; the variable tips form the antigen-binding site, giving each antibody its specificity.

B cells carry surface antibody and, once activated, become plasma cells that secrete it. T cells see antigen fragments displayed on MHC (major histocompatibility complex) molecules: CD4 helper T cells release cytokines that assist B cells, while CD8 cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. A response runs through recognition, clonal expansion, then contraction and memory.

sections.heading: Polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies
sections.text:
Polyclonal antibodies are raised by immunising an animal; its serum holds many antibodies against different epitopes (binding sites) of the antigen. They are cheap and robust, but each batch differs.

Monoclonal antibodies come from one B cell fused with a myeloma cell to form a hybridoma (Köhler and Milstein, 1975). The hybridoma divides indefinitely and secretes one antibody of a single specificity; ELISA screening and limiting dilution isolate the clone.

sections.heading: Immunodiagnostic formats
sections.text:
ELISA uses an enzyme label, commonly horseradish peroxidase, that converts a substrate into a coloured product measured by absorbance. Sandwich ELISA traps antigen between two antibodies; indirect ELISA detects serum antibodies; competitive ELISA measures antigen by its competition with a labelled tracer.

Immunofluorescence tags an antibody with a fluorophore for fluorescence microscopy or flow cytometry. Other formats include Western blot, lateral-flow strips and radioimmunoassay.

Dilution example: 10 mL of 2 µg/mL from a 1 mg/mL stock needs 10 × 2 = 20 µg. The stock is 1000 µg/mL, so pipette 20 µL of stock and make up to 10 mL.

keyPoints: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is specific and keeps memory.
An antibody is a Y-shaped immunoglobulin whose variable tips bind one epitope.
B cells secrete antibody; CD4 helper T cells assist them and CD8 cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells.
Polyclonal antibodies are a mixed serum product; a monoclonal antibody comes from one hybridoma clone.
ELISA uses an enzyme label; sandwich, indirect and competitive formats differ in what is captured.
Volume of stock = (final concentration × final volume) ÷ stock concentration.

en.title: Microbial genetics and strain improvement
en.short: Bacterial mutation, DNA transfer, plasmids, phages and industrial strain improvement.

sections.heading: Mutation and transfer
sections.text:
Mutation is a heritable change in DNA sequence. It may be spontaneous or induced by agents such as ultraviolet light or chemicals. Mutants are useful only if they can be detected and grown.

Bacteria exchange DNA by three routes. Transformation is uptake of free DNA from the surroundings; it needs competent cells, which can take up DNA. Conjugation is transfer of DNA through direct cell contact, often of a plasmid. Transduction is transfer of bacterial DNA by a bacteriophage. These routes spread genes.

sections.heading: Plasmids and transposons
sections.text:
Plasmids are small extrachromosomal DNA molecules that replicate independently of the chromosome. The F plasmid carries genes for conjugation; R plasmids carry antibiotic resistance genes. Plasmids can be lost without selection.

Transposons are DNA segments that can move to new sites in a genome. Insertion sequences are the simplest; composite transposons carry extra genes, such as antibiotic resistance, between insertion sequences. Movement can disrupt genes and cause mutation.

sections.heading: Bacteriophage biology
sections.text:
Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. A virulent phage always follows the lytic cycle: it replicates and bursts the cell. A temperate phage can also enter the lysogenic cycle, inserting its DNA as a prophage and remaining dormant.

Generalized transduction happens when a phage mistakenly packages host DNA instead of phage DNA. Specialized transduction follows imprecise excision of a prophage and carries only nearby host genes.

sections.heading: Strain improvement
sections.text:
Classical strain improvement uses random mutagenesis followed by screening and selection. Screening tests many colonies for the desired trait. Selection uses conditions in which only wanted mutants grow, such as a toxic analogue or an antibiotic.

Molecular improvement makes defined changes: extra copies of a biosynthetic gene, a stronger promoter, or deletion of a competing pathway. Improved strains must be stable and safe.

Example: a lab seeks a protease-producing Bacillus. It treats spores with ultraviolet light, plates them on skim-milk agar, and picks colonies with large clear zones. Flask assays compare protease yield with the parent.

keyPoints: Mutation is a heritable DNA change and can be spontaneous or induced.
Transformation, conjugation and transduction are three routes of bacterial DNA transfer.
Plasmids replicate independently; transposons move within genomes.
Temperate phages can lysogenise and cause specialized transduction.
Classical strain improvement pairs random mutagenesis with screening or selection.
Molecular strain improvement makes defined changes and then tests for stable high-yielding strains.

en.title: Fermentation and bioprocess engineering
en.short: Bioreactor modes, media, oxygen transfer, control, kinetics and scale-up principles.

sections.heading: Vessels and modes
sections.text: A bioreactor is a vessel that keeps cells or enzymes in a controlled environment. Stirred tanks are common; bubble columns and airlift reactors mix by gas, and packed beds hold immobilised cells. Batch culture adds medium once and runs through lag, log, stationary and death phases. Fed-batch adds nutrients during the run, limiting by-product formation and substrate inhibition. Continuous culture feeds fresh medium while removing broth at the same rate; the chemostat reaches steady state when growth rate μ equals dilution rate D = F ÷ V. If D exceeds μmax, cells wash out.

sections.heading: Media and oxygen
sections.text: Medium design supplies carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, trace elements and growth factors, with suitable C:N ratio, pH buffer and antifoam. It must be sterilised without destroying heat-labile parts. Oxygen is sparingly soluble, so supply often limits growth. The oxygen transfer rate is OTR = kLa(C* − C), where kLa is the volumetric mass transfer coefficient, C* is saturation and C is measured concentration. Mixing keeps cells and nutrients uniform and breaks bubbles, but high agitation causes shear. Example: kLa = 50 h⁻¹, C* = 8 mg/L, C = 2 mg/L gives OTR = 50 × (8 − 2) = 300 mg/L/h.

sections.heading: Control and kinetics
sections.text: pH, temperature and dissolved oxygen are measured by probes and held by controllers, usually PID (proportional, integral, derivative). pH is corrected with acid or base, temperature with a jacket, and dissolved oxygen by changing agitation or aeration. Growth kinetics use Monod: μ = μmax S ÷ (Ks + S), where S is the limiting substrate. Product rate qP may be growth-associated, non-growth-associated or mixed: qP = αμ + β.

sections.heading: Scale-up
sections.text: Scale-up moves a process from a small vessel to a larger one without losing performance. Mixing, oxygen transfer and shear do not scale together, so no single rule works. Engineers hold kLa, power per volume, tip speed or mixing time constant, and check with pilot runs and computational fluid dynamics. Oxygen transfer is often limiting.

keyPoints: Batch adds medium once; fed-batch adds nutrients during the run; continuous culture reaches steady state when μ = D = F ÷ V, and washes out if D exceeds μmax.
PID controllers hold pH, temperature and dissolved oxygen at setpoints using acid or base, a jacket, and agitation or aeration.
Oxygen transfer rate is OTR = kLa(C* − C); kLa rises with agitation and aeration, but shear also rises.
Monod growth is μ = μmax S ÷ (Ks + S), where S is the limiting substrate.
Product kinetics can be growth-associated, non-growth-associated or mixed, as in qP = αμ + β.
Scale-up holds a chosen criterion such as kLa or power per volume constant, because no single rule preserves all conditions.

en.title: Downstream processing and product recovery
en.short: Recovery steps from cell disruption to drying, and how stability and economics set their order.

sections.heading: Order and stability
sections.text: Downstream processing (DSP) turns a broth or culture into a stable, pure product. The usual order is harvest, cell disruption if the product is intracellular, clarification, concentration, purification, polishing (final trace-impurity removal) and drying. Stability sets the limits: control temperature and pH, limit shear and time, and inactivate proteases. Economics sets the number of steps. Each step adds equipment, consumables, labour, validation and waste, and loses product. Remove water and contaminants early only if the product survives.

sections.heading: Release and separate
sections.text:
Cell disruption releases intracellular products. High-pressure homogenisation forces cells through a narrow valve; bead mills grind them with small beads; sonication uses ultrasound. Chemical lysis and enzymatic digestion are gentler but add cost and impurities. Choose by scale, heat sensitivity and containment.

Solid-liquid separation removes cells and debris. Centrifugation spins the suspension so denser particles form a pellet or sediment. Filtration passes liquid through a membrane or cake that retains particles. Centrifugation suits fine, sticky solids; filtration suits large volumes and scales easily. Flocculants clump fine cells so they settle faster; filter aids keep fine solids from clogging the filter.

sections.heading: Purify and dry
sections.text:
Extraction moves the product into a chosen solvent. Liquid-liquid extraction uses two immiscible phases; aqueous two-phase systems are gentler for proteins. Precipitation makes the product or a contaminant insoluble by changing salt concentration, solvent or pH, then separates it by centrifugation or filtration.

Chromatography separates molecules by affinity (specific binding), charge or size. A typical train is capture, intermediate purification and polishing. Affinity gives high purity in one step but resin is expensive; ion exchange and size exclusion are cheaper but need more steps.

Example: 1,000 L of broth at 2 g/L contains 2 kg. Yields of 95%, 80% and 90% give 2 × 0.95 × 0.80 × 0.90 = 1.368 kg, an overall yield of 68.4%.

Drying removes water for stability and lower shipping cost. Freeze-drying sublimes ice under vacuum and suits heat-sensitive proteins; spray drying is faster and cheaper but hotter.

keyPoints: Downstream processing order is harvest, cell disruption if needed, clarification, concentration, purification, polishing and drying.
Cell disruption methods include high-pressure homogenisation, bead milling, sonication, chemical lysis and enzymatic digestion; choose by scale and heat sensitivity.
Centrifugation and filtration separate solids from liquid; centrifugation suits fine sticky solids, filtration suits large volumes.
Extraction and precipitation concentrate or partly purify the product before chromatography.
Chromatography separates by affinity, charge or size and is usually arranged as capture, intermediate purification and polishing.
Overall yield = product of step yields; for 0.95 × 0.80 × 0.90 the result is 0.684, or 68.4%.

en.title: Industrial biotechnology and bioproducts
en.short: Strains, process routes and quality for antibiotics, enzymes, acids, amino acids, vitamins, biopolymers and biofuels.

sections.heading: Products and strains
sections.text:
Industrial biotechnology uses cells or enzymes to make products at large scale. Main groups are antibiotics (for example penicillin from Penicillium), industrial enzymes (proteases, amylases), organic acids (citric, lactic), amino acids (glutamate, lysine), vitamins (riboflavin, B12), biopolymers (polyhydroxyalkanoates, xanthan) and biofuels (ethanol, biodiesel).

Strain choice decides titre (g/L), yield (g product/g substrate) and productivity (g/L/h). A good strain grows on cheap feedstock, secretes product, is stable and safe. Examples: Aspergillus niger for citric acid, Corynebacterium glutamicum for amino acids, Bacillus species for enzymes, Saccharomyces cerevisiae for ethanol. Regulation and the market decide whether a natural, GRAS (United States safety status) or recombinant strain is acceptable.

sections.heading: Process routes
sections.text:
Routes suit the product. Submerged fermentation in stirred tanks is common for antibiotics, enzymes and amino acids. Solid-state fermentation suits some fungi and enzymes. Batch, fed-batch and continuous operation trade simplicity against productivity. Whole cells suit products that need many enzymes; isolated enzymes suit a clean single reaction.

Example: a citric acid plant uses A. niger in a fed-batch fermenter with 200 m³ working volume. Suppose titre is 150 g/L and recovery is 85%. Product per batch = 150 kg/m³ × 200 m³ = 30,000 kg = 30 t. With about 60 batches per year, output = 30 × 60 × 0.85 = 1,530 t/year. Volumetric productivity = 150 g/L ÷ 120 h = 1.25 g/L/h.

sections.heading: Quality requirements
sections.text: Quality depends on use. Pharmaceutical antibiotics need identity, potency and, for injectables, sterility and low endotoxin, with pharmacopoeial monographs (official drug standards) and Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP). Food and feed enzymes need declared activity, low microbial contamination and heavy-metal limits; GRAS or novel-food status depends on the country. Amino acids and vitamins need purity and assay limits. Biopolymers need defined molecular weight and monomer composition. Biofuels must meet national fuel standards, such as ASTM D6751 for biodiesel. Every product needs batch records, a certificate of analysis and batch-to-batch consistency.

keyPoints: Industrial biotechnology makes antibiotics, enzymes, organic acids, amino acids, vitamins, biopolymers and biofuels using cells or enzymes.
Strain choice balances titre, yield, productivity, genetic stability, safety and feedstock cost.
Submerged fermentation is common; solid-state, whole-cell and isolated-enzyme routes suit particular products.
Annual output = titre × working volume × batches per year × recovery.
Volumetric productivity = titre ÷ fermentation time, usually in g/L/h.
Quality follows use: GMP and pharmacopoeial tests for medicines, activity and contaminant limits for food enzymes, and fuel standards for biofuels.

en.title: Environmental biotechnology: waste treatment, bioremediation and biosensors
en.short: Activated sludge, anaerobic digestion, bioremediation, composting, biosensors and bioindicators.

sections.heading: Activated sludge
sections.text:
Wastewater treatment screens and settles solids, then treats the rest biologically. Activated sludge is an aerobic suspended-growth process: bacteria, including floc-formers such as Zoogloea, grow in an aerated tank and clump into flocs, while protozoa graze on free cells. The mix flows to a clarifier; settled sludge is returned to hold biomass, and surplus is wasted. Operators control sludge age and the food-to-microorganism ratio.

Example: influent BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) 300 mg/L, effluent 20 mg/L. Removal = (300 − 20) ÷ 300 × 100 = 93.3%.

sections.heading: Anaerobic digestion
sections.text:
Anaerobic digestion treats sludge and strong waste without oxygen. Microbes work in sequence: hydrolysis breaks polymers, acidogens make volatile fatty acids, acetogens make acetate, and methanogens, which are archaea, make methane. Methanogens grow slowly and need near-neutral pH and warmth, often about 35 °C. Biogas is roughly 60% methane and 40% carbon dioxide, though this varies with feedstock.

Example: the theoretical yield is about 0.35 m³ of methane per kg of COD (chemical oxygen demand) removed at standard conditions.

sections.heading: Bioremediation and composting
sections.text:
Bioremediation uses organisms to remove contaminants. Intrinsic bioremediation relies on native microbes; biostimulation adds nutrients or oxygen; bioaugmentation adds selected cultures. Aerobic degradation suits petroleum hydrocarbons; anaerobic reductive dechlorination suits some chlorinated solvents. Phytoremediation uses plants to extract or stabilise metals.

Composting is aerobic solid-phase treatment. Thermophilic bacteria and fungi raise the temperature and kill pathogens. A carbon-to-nitrogen ratio near 25–30 to 1, moisture of 50–60% and regular turning keep it working.

Illustrative case: fuel-contaminated soil at a depot in Kano is tilled, fertilised and monitored until hydrocarbon levels fall.

sections.heading: Biosensors and bioindicators
sections.text:
A biosensor couples a biological recognition element, such as an enzyme, antibody or whole cell, to a transducer, which may be electrochemical or optical. The reaction gives a signal proportional to analyte concentration, and the sensor is calibrated with standards. A BOD biosensor uses immobilised microbes and measures their respiration.

Bioindicators are organisms whose presence or condition reveals environmental quality: mayfly larvae suggest clean streams, lichens are sensitive to sulphur dioxide, and algal blooms suggest nutrient enrichment.

keyPoints: Activated sludge is an aerobic suspended-growth process controlled by sludge age and the food-to-microorganism ratio.
Anaerobic digestion runs through hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis and methanogenesis; methanogens are slow-growing archaea.
Theoretical methane yield is about 0.35 m³ per kg of COD removed at standard conditions.
Biostimulation adds nutrients or oxygen; bioaugmentation adds selected microbial cultures.
Composting needs a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio near 25–30 to 1, moisture of 50–60% and aeration.
A biosensor pairs a biorecognition element with a transducer; a bioindicator is an organism that signals environmental quality.

en.title: Plant and agricultural biotechnology
en.short: Tissue culture, transformation, GM traits, markers and biocontrol, with agricultural biosafety.

sections.heading: Tissue culture and micropropagation
sections.text:
Plant tissue culture grows plant cells or organs on a sterile nutrient medium under controlled light and temperature. A small piece of tissue, the explant, is surface-sterilised and placed on medium with sugars, minerals and plant hormones. The balance of auxin to cytokinin decides whether shoots or roots form.

Micropropagation makes many identical plantlets from one explant by repeated subculture, meaning transfer to fresh medium. It multiplies elite or disease-free stock quickly, as in banana and cassava planting material. Somaclonal variation, off-types arising in culture, is a risk.

sections.heading: Transformation and GM crops
sections.text:
Genetic transformation inserts a foreign gene into plant cells. Agrobacterium tumefaciens carries the gene on its Ti (tumour-inducing) plasmid and transfers it into the cell. The gene gun shoots DNA-coated metal particles into cells. Both methods need a selectable marker and regeneration of whole plants from transformed cells.

GM crops carry traits such as insect resistance from Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) genes, herbicide tolerance, virus resistance or improved nutrition. Each trait must be shown to be stable and safe for non-target organisms.

sections.heading: Molecular markers
sections.text: Molecular markers are DNA sequences that vary between individuals and are easy to score, such as SSRs (simple sequence repeats) and SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms). Marker-assisted selection uses a marker closely linked to a useful gene to choose seedlings early, without waiting for the plant to mature or be exposed to disease. It speeds breeding, but only when the marker-trait link has been validated in that population.

sections.heading: Biofertilisers, biopesticides, biosafety
sections.text:
Biofertilisers are preparations of living microbes that improve nutrient supply, such as rhizobia fixing nitrogen in legume nodules or mycorrhizal fungi helping roots take up phosphorus. Biopesticides use living organisms or their products, such as Bacillus thuringiensis spores, to control pests.

Biosafety questions specific to agriculture: gene flow to wild relatives and neighbouring farms, effects on non-target insects and soil life, build-up of resistant pests, and labelling and coexistence rules. Rules differ by country, so check the national biosafety authority.

keyPoints: Micropropagation clones one explant into many plantlets on sterile hormone-balanced medium.
Agrobacterium and the gene gun are the two standard ways to transform plant cells.
GM traits such as Bt insect resistance must be stable and tested for non-target effects.
Marker-assisted selection chooses seedlings using a validated marker linked to a useful gene.
Biofertilisers supply nutrients through living microbes; biopesticides control pests with living agents or their products.
Agricultural biosafety centres on gene flow, non-target effects and resistant pests, and rules vary by country.

en.title: Medical and pharmaceutical biotechnology
en.short: Recombinant proteins, vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, gene therapy, diagnostics and the path to approval.

sections.heading: Therapeutic proteins
sections.text: Recombinant therapeutic proteins are proteins made by cells whose DNA has been altered to carry the human gene. The first licensed example was human insulin produced in bacteria, approved in 1982. Such proteins treat diabetes, anaemia and some cancers. Because they match the natural human protein more closely than animal-derived products, they usually cause fewer immune reactions. Production uses bacteria, yeast or mammalian cells, and the product must be purified and tested for identity, potency and safety.

sections.heading: Vaccines and antibodies
sections.text: A vaccine platform is the technology used to present an antigen, a substance the immune system recognises. Main platforms include live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, toxoid, viral vector, mRNA and DNA vaccines. Each balances safety, stability and the type of immune response. Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibody molecules from one clone of cells. They bind one epitope, a specific target site, with high specificity and are used for cancer, autoimmune disease and some infections. Humanised or fully human antibodies are less likely to be attacked by the patient’s immune system.

sections.heading: Gene therapy and diagnostics
sections.text: Gene therapy delivers genetic material to treat or prevent disease. It may add a working gene, silence a faulty one or edit DNA. Vectors are often viruses, but non-viral methods are also used. Treatment can be ex vivo (cells removed, modified and returned) or in vivo (delivered directly). Molecular diagnostics detect DNA or RNA to confirm infection, identify mutations or guide treatment. Common methods include PCR, nucleic acid hybridisation and sequencing. Antigen tests detect proteins and are related immunoassays rather than molecular methods.

sections.heading: From candidate to licence
sections.text: A candidate molecule goes through preclinical testing in cells and animals to assess safety, toxicity and dose. If it passes, clinical trials begin. Phase I tests safety in a small group. Phase II tests efficacy and side effects in patients. Phase III compares the candidate with existing treatment in a larger group. Regulators then review the evidence. Approval rules differ by country, so check the national regulator, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria or the FDA in the United States. After approval, post-marketing surveillance continues.

keyPoints: Recombinant therapeutic proteins are made by genetically modified cells and include human insulin, approved in 1982.
Vaccine platforms include live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, toxoid, viral vector, mRNA and DNA vaccines.
Monoclonal antibodies are identical molecules that bind one epitope and are used for cancer, autoimmune disease and infections.
Gene therapy delivers genetic material to add, silence or edit genes, using viral or non-viral vectors.
Molecular diagnostics detect DNA or RNA by methods such as PCR, hybridisation and sequencing; antigen tests detect proteins instead.
A medicine passes preclinical testing, then Phase I to III trials, then regulatory approval, which varies by country.

en.title: Food biotechnology: fermentation, testing and regulation
en.short: Fermented foods, starter cultures, enzymes, probiotics, molecular food testing and novel food rules.

sections.heading: Fermented foods and cultures
sections.text:
Fermented foods are made by microorganisms that change sugars and other compounds, lowering pH or producing alcohol, acids or flavours. Examples include yoghurt, cheese, bread, beer, soy sauce, and in West Africa ogi (maize), garri (cassava) and iru (locust bean).

A starter culture is a defined preparation of live microorganisms added to start fermentation reliably. It may be one strain or a mix, and it gives control over taste, safety and speed. Traditional fermentations often rely on wild microbes; commercial ones use selected starters.

sections.heading: Enzymes, additives and probiotics
sections.text:
Food enzymes are proteins used as processing aids: rennet (chymosin) clots milk, amylases break down starch, and pectinases clear fruit juice. Additives are substances added for a technical purpose, such as preservatives, colours or emulsifiers; most countries allow only those on a positive list.

Probiotics are live microorganisms that, in adequate amounts, give a health benefit to the host (FAO/WHO definition). Health claims are regulated in most countries, so a product cannot promise benefits without evidence and approval.

sections.heading: Molecular food testing
sections.text:
Molecular methods detect specific DNA or proteins. PCR and real-time PCR can find pathogens such as Salmonella or Listeria in food, and can identify species in meat, fish or honey. DNA barcoding uses a standard gene region to identify species.

A case: a beef product is tested by real-time PCR with a pork-specific probe; a positive signal shows undeclared pork, which matters for fraud and for religious or cultural diets. ELISA is a common antibody-based alternative for proteins.

sections.heading: Spoilage, preservation, regulation
sections.text:
Spoilage is any change that makes food unfit or unacceptable, caused by microbial growth, enzymes or oxidation. Preservation slows these: heat, cold, drying, salting, acidification, modified atmosphere packaging and irradiation.

Novel foods are foods not significantly used before a set date, or made by a new process. They need pre-market safety assessment. Rules differ: the EU has Regulation 2015/2283, the US uses GRAS status with voluntary FDA notification, and Nigeria requires NAFDAC approval. Always check the current national rule.

keyPoints: Fermented foods are made by microorganisms; starter cultures are defined live cultures added for reliable control.
Probiotics are live microorganisms that give a health benefit when taken in adequate amounts.
Food enzymes are processing aids, while additives are regulated, usually through positive lists.
PCR and DNA barcoding can detect pathogens and identify species for food authenticity.
Spoilage is caused by microbial growth, enzymes and oxidation; preservation slows these processes.
Novel foods need pre-market safety assessment, and the rules vary by country.

en.title: Bioethics, biosafety and regulation
en.short: Ethics of gene editing and testing, patents on life, consent, benefit sharing, and biosafety rules.

sections.heading: Ethics of modification
sections.text: Genetic modification and gene editing raise questions of safety, purpose and justice. Somatic edits change body cells and affect only the patient. Germline edits change eggs, sperm or embryos and are inherited, so they are widely opposed. Human genetic testing can reveal useful risks but also cause stigma or insurance discrimination. In 2018 a researcher in China used CRISPR-Cas9 to edit embryos, and twins were born; the work was condemned as premature and unsafe.

sections.heading: Consent and benefit sharing
sections.text: Informed consent means people understand the purpose, risks, benefits and alternatives before they agree. For genetic testing, confidentiality and the return of incidental findings matter. Benefit sharing means fair distribution of gains from research or from genetic resources. The Nagoya Protocol (2010) governs access to genetic resources and fair benefit sharing. With vulnerable groups, consent must be genuine and free from coercion.

sections.heading: Patents on living things
sections.text: Patents give temporary exclusive rights for inventions that are new, inventive and useful. Whether living things can be patented varies by country. In the United States, Diamond v. Chakrabarty (1980) allowed a patent on a genetically modified bacterium. The WTO’s TRIPS Agreement lets countries exclude plants and animals from patenting but requires protection of plant varieties. Rules on human genes differ and have changed; check national law.

sections.heading: Biosafety and containment
sections.text: Biosafety levels BSL-1 to BSL-4 classify laboratories by risk. BSL-1 is basic; BSL-4 handles dangerous pathogens with maximum containment. Containment has primary measures (good practice, protective equipment, safety cabinets) and secondary measures (facility design, air handling). The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety (2000) regulates transboundary movement of living modified organisms (LMOs). It uses advance informed agreement and a Biosafety Clearing-House. National laws, such as Nigeria’s National Biosafety Management Agency Act 2015, put these rules into practice.

keyPoints: Somatic gene edits affect only the patient; germline edits are inherited and widely opposed.
Informed consent requires understanding purpose, risks and alternatives, and protecting confidentiality.
Benefit sharing means fair distribution of gains from research and genetic resources; the Nagoya Protocol covers this.
Patenting living things varies by country; TRIPS allows excluding plants and animals but requires plant variety protection.
BSL-1 to BSL-4 classify containment by risk, from basic to maximum.
The Cartagena Protocol regulates transboundary movement of LMOs through advance informed agreement.

en.title: Bioinformatics and omics analysis
en.short: Genome annotation, comparative genomics, omics workflows, databases and reporting of large data.

sections.heading: Genome annotation
sections.text: Annotation turns an assembled genome into a list of features. Structural annotation finds genes, exons and regulatory regions. Functional annotation attaches evidence: sequence similarity, protein domains and experimental data. Tools such as BLAST compare sequences, HMMER uses profile hidden Markov models to find domains, and InterPro combines domain databases. Automatic calls are hypotheses; manual review and evidence codes matter. A gene predicted only by software should not be reported as confirmed.

sections.heading: Comparative genomics
sections.text: Comparative genomics compares two or more genomes. Orthologues are genes in different species that diverged from a common ancestral gene after speciation; paralogues arise by gene duplication. Conserved regions may be functional; rearrangements and gene loss show evolution. Align whole genomes or proteins, build trees, and check synteny (gene order). Example: comparing a crop variety with a wild relative can show lost genes, but a difference is not proof of function.

sections.heading: Omics workflows
sections.text: Transcriptomics measures RNA, usually by RNA sequencing. Workflow: design with replicates, extract RNA, check quality, make libraries, sequence, trim and align reads, count per gene, then test differential expression. Proteomics measures proteins, often by liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry. Workflow: extract, digest, separate, ionise, fragment, match spectra to a protein database, then quantify.
