Metabolomics measures small molecules by mass spectrometry or nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR). Workflow: quench, extract, separate and detect, annotate peaks, then analyse. Each step adds noise; keep raw data and metadata.

sections.heading: Databases and reporting
sections.text: Public databases store sequences and results: GenBank and ENA for nucleotides, UniProt for proteins, PDB for structures, GO and KEGG for function and pathways, GEO for expression, PRIDE for proteomics and MetaboLights for metabolomics. Good reporting states the design, sample handling, software versions, thresholds and effect sizes, not only p values. Deposit raw data, share code and describe limits. A case: Ngozi, a student comparing maize samples, must record variety, tissue, stage and batch, or results cannot be reproduced.

keyPoints: Genome annotation predicts features and attaches evidence; automatic calls are hypotheses.
Orthologues diverged from a common ancestral gene after speciation; paralogues arise by gene duplication.
Transcriptomics workflows go from RNA extraction and sequencing to alignment, counting and differential expression.
Proteomics and metabolomics often use mass spectrometry (or NMR for metabolites) with database or spectral matching, and careful annotation.
Public repositories such as GenBank, UniProt, GEO, PRIDE and MetaboLights make data reusable.
Report design, metadata, software versions, thresholds and effect sizes, and deposit raw data.

en.title: Biotechnology enterprise and technology transfer
en.short: IP, freedom to operate, licensing, spin-outs, and planning and costing a bioproduct from lab to market.

sections.heading: IP for biology
sections.text: Intellectual property (IP) means legal rights that protect creations such as inventions. For biological inventions the main tools are patents, trade secrets and know-how, and plant variety rights. A patent gives a limited monopoly in one country in exchange for disclosure. The invention must be new, involve an inventive step and be industrially applicable; what is patentable varies by country, so check national law. Where living material is hard to describe, many systems allow deposit with an approved culture collection.

sections.heading: Freedom to operate
sections.text: Freedom to operate (FTO) means making, using and selling a product without infringing third-party IP in relevant countries. It is not patentability: your invention may be new yet fall inside another patent’s claims. FTO work searches patents and applications, then reads the claims. Record jurisdictions, expiry dates and licences. If a blocking patent exists, design around it, license it or wait for expiry. An FTO opinion is a risk assessment, not a guarantee.

sections.heading: Licensing and spin-outs
sections.text: Licensing lets the IP owner grant rights. A licence may be exclusive or non-exclusive, limited by territory and field of use, and may include upfront fees, milestones, royalties, sublicensing and diligence obligations. A spin-out is a new company formed to commercialise research. The institution assigns or licenses IP to it, founders take equity, and investors fund development. Clear ownership and realistic valuation matter. Material transfer agreements govern materials before licensing.

sections.heading: From lab to market
sections.text:
Moving a laboratory result to industry needs a project plan with technical, regulatory and commercial stages. Estimate capital cost (equipment, facilities), operating cost (materials, staff, utilities) and cost of goods per unit. Include contingency and scale-up losses. Commercial constraints include market size and price, regulatory approval, good manufacturing practice, supply chain, freedom to operate and time to market.

Example: a 100 L pilot run at 1 g/L gives 100 g crude. At 50% recovery, purified product is 50 g. If variable cost is 20,000 currency units, cost is 20,000 ÷ 50 = 400 per gram. At 80% recovery it is 80 g and 250 per gram, so yield matters.

keyPoints: IP rights for biological inventions include patents, trade secrets and know-how, and plant variety rights; patentability varies by country.
A patent must be new, inventive and industrially applicable, and it is territorial.
Freedom to operate means avoiding infringement of third-party IP in each market; it is separate from patentability.
Licences can be exclusive or non-exclusive and are limited by territory, field and payment terms.
A spin-out commercialises research through a new company, with IP assignment or licence, equity and investment.
Cost per unit = total batch cost ÷ purified product mass; recovery and scale-up losses strongly affect it.

en.title: Advanced molecular genetics and genome editing
en.short: Gene regulation, epigenetics, CRISPR and other editors, delivery, off-targets and validation.

sections.heading: Regulating genes
sections.text:
Gene regulation controls when, where and how strongly a gene is expressed. It works through promoters, enhancers, silencers, transcription factors, RNA processing, stability and translation. Epigenetics is heritable change in gene activity without a change in DNA sequence. Main mechanisms are DNA methylation at CpG sites, histone modification, chromatin remodelling and non-coding RNAs. These marks alter chromatin accessibility.

CRISPR interference (CRISPRi) and activation (CRISPRa) use inactive Cas9 fused to a repressor or activator to test regulatory elements without cutting DNA.

sections.heading: Editing systems
sections.text: CRISPR-Cas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes uses a guide RNA (sgRNA) to direct Cas9 to DNA beside a protospacer adjacent motif (PAM), usually NGG. Cas9 cuts both strands, making a double-strand break. Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repairs the break and often leaves insertions or deletions (indels). Homology-directed repair (HDR) can copy a template. Base editors change one base without a double-strand break; prime editors write sequences using reverse transcriptase. ZFNs, TALENs and meganucleases are protein-guided nucleases that also create targeted breaks.

sections.heading: Designing experiments
sections.text:
Design begins with the aim: knockout, knock-in, repression or base change. Choose the system, target site, PAM and predicted off-targets, and plan controls. Delivery can be plasmid DNA, mRNA or preformed Cas9-sgRNA ribonucleoprotein (RNP). Methods include electroporation, lipofection, microinjection and viral vectors. RNP delivery is short-lived and can reduce off-target activity. Off-target effects occur at similar sites; predict them computationally and test the most likely ones.

Case: to knock out a gene in a human cell line, use two sgRNAs against early exons, deliver RNPs by electroporation, and include a non-targeting sgRNA control.

sections.heading: Validating edits
sections.text: Validate at DNA, RNA and protein levels. For indels, PCR-amplify the target and use Sanger sequencing with indel analysis or amplicon deep sequencing. For HDR knock-in, use junction PCR and sequencing. Check predicted off-target sites by targeted deep sequencing; unbiased methods such as GUIDE-seq or CIRCLE-seq can find unexpected sites. Confirm loss of function by RT-qPCR and protein assay. Compare edited and unedited cells from the same passage, with repeats and independent clones.

keyPoints: Epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation and histone modification change chromatin state without changing DNA sequence.
CRISPR-Cas9 uses an sgRNA and a PAM to make a double-strand break, repaired by NHEJ (indels) or HDR (template copy).
Base and prime editors make changes without a double-strand break; ZFNs, TALENs and meganucleases are protein-guided alternatives.
Delivery as RNP, mRNA or plasmid, by electroporation, lipofection, microinjection or viral vectors, affects duration and off-target risk.
Off-target effects are predicted computationally and tested by targeted deep sequencing or unbiased assays such as GUIDE-seq.
Validate edits by PCR plus Sanger or deep sequencing, junction PCR for knock-ins, and RNA and protein assays with proper controls.

en.title: Systems and synthetic biology
en.short: Network analysis, gene circuit models, synthetic devices, chassis and standards.

sections.heading: Networks and motifs
sections.text: Systems biology studies biological networks as sets of nodes and edges. In a gene regulatory network, nodes are genes or proteins and edges are activating or repressing interactions. Analysis looks for motifs such as feedback loops and feed-forward loops, and for properties such as robustness (stability under disturbance), modularity (separable units) and bistability (two stable states). A motif is a small recurring wiring pattern. These properties describe the network as a whole, not one gene alone.

sections.heading: Modelling gene circuits
sections.text: Mathematical models turn a circuit diagram into equations. Deterministic models use ordinary differential equations (ODEs); stochastic models use probabilities when molecule numbers are low. A Hill function describes cooperative activation or repression. For repression, dP/dt = α ÷ (1 + (R ÷ K)ⁿ) − δP, where α is the maximum production rate, δ the degradation rate, R the repressor concentration, K the repression threshold and n the cooperativity. At steady state P* = α ÷ (δ(1 + (R ÷ K)ⁿ)). Example: α = 100 molecules per minute, δ = 0.1 per minute, R = K, n = 2. Then P* = 100 ÷ (0.1 × 2) = 500 molecules. Boolean models simplify genes to on or off.

sections.heading: Design and construction
sections.text: Synthetic biology designs and builds genetic devices from standard parts. A device might be a sensor, a logic gate or an oscillator. Parts include promoters, ribosome binding sites, coding sequences and terminators. Standards such as BioBricks assembly and SBOL, the Synthetic Biology Open Language, help share and reuse designs. A chassis organism is the host cell, often Escherichia coli or yeast, in which the device runs. Its physiology affects the device.

sections.heading: Limits and standards
sections.text: Prediction is limited. Device behaviour depends on the chassis, growth conditions and genetic context. Cells carry a burden when a circuit uses resources, and mutations can break the device. Noise causes cell-to-cell variation, and many model parameters are uncertain or not identifiable from data. Standards improve reproducibility but do not guarantee function. Build, test and revise in the chosen chassis, and treat model predictions as hypotheses.

keyPoints: Systems biology analyses networks through nodes, edges and recurring motifs such as feedback and feed-forward loops.
Deterministic gene circuit models use ODEs; stochastic models are needed when molecule numbers are low.
For Hill repression, dP/dt = α ÷ (1 + (R ÷ K)ⁿ) − δP, so P* = α ÷ (δ(1 + (R ÷ K)ⁿ)).
Synthetic devices are built from standard parts such as promoters, ribosome binding sites, coding sequences and terminators.
BioBricks assembly and SBOL are standards for sharing and reusing synthetic biology designs.
Chassis context, burden, noise, mutation and uncertain parameters limit prediction, so designs must be tested and revised.

en.title: Metabolic engineering and strain design
en.short: Redesigning microbial metabolism by rational and evolutionary methods, flux analysis and genome-scale models.

sections.heading: Rational and evolutionary
sections.text: Metabolic engineering is the deliberate modification of a cell’s metabolism to make a product. Rational design uses known biochemistry: delete genes that divert carbon or redox power, overexpress bottleneck enzymes, and introduce a heterologous pathway. The design-build-test-learn cycle repeats with measurements. Evolutionary approaches use selection instead. Adaptive laboratory evolution (ALE) serially transfers cells under a chosen pressure, such as growth on a poor carbon source or tolerance to a toxic product, and selects faster variants. Random mutagenesis and screening is another route. Rational design is faster when the pathway is known; evolution can find hard-to-predict changes.

sections.heading: Flux and balance
sections.text: Flux is the rate of metabolite conversion. Metabolic flux analysis (MFA) estimates intracellular fluxes from isotope labelling and extracellular rates. Flux balance analysis (FBA) uses a stoichiometric network and solves for fluxes that optimise an objective, often growth or product secretion, subject to mass balance and capacity constraints. At steady state, Σ Sij vj = 0, where S is the stoichiometric matrix and v the flux vector. Pathway balancing matches enzyme levels, cofactors such as NADPH and ATP, and precursor supply so no step limits the others; tunable promoters and ribosome binding sites help.

sections.heading: Genome-scale models
sections.text: Genome-scale models (GEMs) are stoichiometric reconstructions of all known reactions in an organism. FBA on a GEM predicts growth, by-product secretion and gene deletions, and suggests knockout targets. Models are hypotheses: they need experimental validation because regulation, kinetics and transport are simplified. They help rank designs before lab work.

sections.heading: Yield example
sections.text: Yield is product mass per substrate mass consumed. For glucose to ethanol: C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2. Molar masses are 180.16 g/mol for glucose and 46.07 g/mol for ethanol. Theoretical yield = (2 × 46.07) ÷ 180.16 = 0.511 g/g. From 100 g glucose the maximum is 51.1 g ethanol. If a strain makes 45 g, yield = 0.45 g/g, 88% of theoretical. Useful strains also need high titre (g/L) and productivity (g/L/h), not yield alone.

keyPoints: Metabolic engineering changes metabolism deliberately; rational design edits known steps, while ALE and mutagenesis use selection.
At steady state, Σ Sij vj = 0; FBA optimises an objective such as growth or product flux under constraints.
Pathway balancing matches enzyme expression, cofactors and precursors to avoid bottlenecks and toxic intermediates.
Genome-scale models predict knockout effects but need experimental validation.
Yield = product mass ÷ substrate mass; titre is g/L and productivity is g/L/h.
Glucose to ethanol has a theoretical yield of 0.511 g/g: (2 × 46.07) ÷ 180.16.

en.title: Research methods and the dissertation
en.short: Framing a research question, reviewing literature, choosing methods, ethics, data and defending a dissertation.

sections.heading: Framing the question
sections.text: A research question is the uncertainty your dissertation will reduce. A good one is answerable with your time, samples, equipment and skills, and names the population, variable and comparison. Turn it into a testable hypothesis or, for exploratory work, a clear aim. Example: Chidi studies antibiotic resistance on poultry farms. 'Is resistance increasing?' is too broad. A workable question asks whether, on broiler farms in one district, the proportion of Escherichia coli isolates resistant to a named antibiotic is higher on farms using that antibiotic as a growth promoter than on farms not using it. The wording must match what you can sample.

sections.heading: Literature and methods
sections.text:
Critically reviewing literature maps what is known, where studies disagree, and which methods produced the evidence. Use primary papers and reviews; record search terms, databases and inclusion rules so the review is reproducible. Compare designs, sample sizes and limitations, and show the gap your question fills.

Choose experimental methods when you can manipulate variables and control confounders; choose computational methods when suitable data exist or experiments are impractical. Justify by validity, cost, time and ethics; pilot the protocol.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text:
Biotechnology research needs approval before sampling. An institutional research ethics committee reviews risks to people and communities; animal work may need separate animal ethics approval; a biosafety committee reviews genetically modified organisms, pathogens and waste. Rules differ by country; check your institution and national regulator. Consent, confidentiality and fair benefit sharing must be planned, not added later.

Write a data management plan: what you collect, file formats, naming, storage, backup, access and retention. Fix analysis methods in advance; report effect sizes and confidence intervals, not only p values. Keep raw data and analysis scripts.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text: Write the dissertation as an argument: introduction and question, literature, methods, results, discussion, conclusion. Report methods so another student could repeat them. At the viva (oral defence), examiners test whether you understand your choices and limits. Rehearse why each method was chosen, what could bias results, and what you would change.

keyPoints: A research question should name the population, variable and comparison, and be answerable with available resources.
A critical literature review compares study designs and limitations, records search methods, and identifies the gap.
Choose experimental methods for controlled manipulation and computational methods for suitable existing data; justify by validity, cost, time and ethics.
Ethics and biosafety approval must come before sampling; rules vary by country, so check institutional and national requirements.
A data management plan covers collection, formats, storage, backup, access and retention; fix analysis methods in advance and keep raw data and scripts.
Write the dissertation as an argument and prepare for the viva by explaining and defending your methodological choices.
